text_blocks.snippet: Legionnaires' disease is caused by Legionella bacteria, most commonly Legionella pneumophila. These bacteria thrive in warm water environments and can be found in various man-made water systems. People contract the illness by inhaling mist or water droplets containing the bacteria, not by drinking contaminated water.
snippet_highlighted_words: Legionella bacteria, most commonly Legionella pneumophila

list.snippet: Legionella bacteria are the causative agent of Legionnaires' disease.
Legionella pneumophila is the most common species responsible.
These bacteria are naturally found in water sources but can multiply in man-made water systems.
Legionnaires' disease is not spread through person-to-person contact.
It is contracted by inhaling aerosols (tiny water droplets) containing the bacteria.
These aerosols can be produced by various water sources, including:
Cooling towers (often part of large air conditioning systems).
Hot tubs and whirlpools.
Showers and faucets.
Decorative fountains.
Humidifiers.
The bacteria can also be found in potting mixes, and Legionnaires' disease has been linked to inhaling contaminated potting mix dust.
While most people exposed to Legionella do not develop the disease, certain individuals are at higher risk.
These include:
People aged 50 years or older.
Current or former smokers.
Individuals with chronic lung diseases (like COPD or emphysema).
People with weakened immune systems (due to diseases like cancer, HIV, or medications that suppress the immune system).
Those with other underlying medical conditions (like diabetes, kidney or liver disease).
Individuals living in long-term care facilities or those who have recently been hospitalized.
Legionnaires' disease is a severe form of pneumonia, causing flu-like symptoms and potentially leading to respiratory failure, kidney failure, or other complications.
Pontiac fever is a milder, flu-like illness caused by Legionella bacteria, but it is not the same as Legionnaires' disease.

text_blocks.snippet: Legionnaires' disease outbreaks are happening around the world, including a recent one in Grand Rapids, Minnesota. The disease is caused by Legionella bacteria and can lead to a severe form of pneumonia. Outbreaks often occur in places with warm water systems like cooling towers and hot tubs.
snippet_highlighted_words: Legionnaires' disease outbreaks are happening around the world, including a recent one in Grand Rapids, Minnesota

list.title: Grand Rapids, Minnesota:
list.snippet: An outbreak from April 2023 to June 2024 resulted in 34 cases, with 30 hospitalizations and 2 deaths. The municipal water system was identified as the source, and a chlorine disinfection system was implemented.

list.title: Cruise Ships:
list.snippet: The CDC investigated two outbreaks among cruise ship passengers, with hot tubs on cabin balconies identified as the likely source.

list.title: Other Outbreaks:
list.snippet: Various locations, including Warren (Michigan), Richmond (California), and New Glasgow (Canada), have also experienced Legionnaires' disease outbreaks.

list.title: Cause:
list.snippet: It's a bacterial infection caused by Legionella bacteria, primarily contracted by inhaling aerosolized water containing the bacteria.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Legionnaires' disease causes pneumonia, while a milder form called Pontiac fever causes flu-like symptoms.

list.title: Risk Factors:
list.snippet: Individuals with weakened immune systems, chronic lung conditions, or those over 50 are at higher risk.

list.title: Outbreak Definition:
list.snippet: An outbreak is defined as two or more cases with a common exposure within a six-week period.
Investigation: Outbreak investigations involve identifying the source, environmental sampling, and implementing control measures.
Treatment: Legionnaires' disease is treated with antibiotics.
Prevention: Maintaining water systems, regular cleaning, and proper use of water-related devices (like humidifiers) can help prevent Legionella growth.
